solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Very articulate precursor of Selassie

indicators.note: to articulate a word is to speak it, so the name is said out loud here

parts.note: the Ethiopian emperor was Haile Selassie, so his first name comes before Selassie

explanation.surface: A puzzling request for the eloquent forerunner of an Ethiopian emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulate' poses as an adjective meaning eloquent, but it is the speaking signal: HAILE, the first name of Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, is pronounced like 'highly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are intensifying adverbs: very good and extremely good mean the same.

clue.text: Make husky turn north, east and south after frost

indicators.note: the reversed compass points come after the frost word

parts.note: hoar is hoar frost, white frost

indicators.note: turn means the three compass letters are read in the opposite order

explanation.surface: Instructions for a sled dog to turn around after the frost sets in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husky' suggests the sled dog; it means rough-voiced.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a voice rough and croaky, as a sore throat does.

clue.text: Bombastic bully adores gin

indicators.note: to bully is to push around, so the letters are pushed into a new order

explanation.surface: A pompous tyrant loves his gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' poses as a noun but is the verb, telling us to knock the letters about.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandiose speech is pompous and inflated, just like bombast.

clue.text: Punjabis here learning to restrain sigh?

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in, so the learning word holds the sigh

parts.note: lore is learning or traditional knowledge
ah is a sigh

explanation.surface: Students from the Punjab sigh as they study.
explanation.definitionFit: Lahore is the capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab, where many Punjabis live.

clue.text: Sketch of Charles I's pony scampering backwards

indicators.note: backwards says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A drawing of a king's little horse galloping in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters SISPONYS sit inside 'Charles I's pony scampering'; read backwards they give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A summary outline of a story or plan, which is what a rough sketch of it gives.

clue.text: Interminably long revolutionary period

indicators.note: interminably means without its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to long is to yearn

explanation.surface: A tediously long time of revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests political upheaval but refers to the Earth's orbit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earth makes one revolution round the Sun in this period.

clue.text: Old vicar gets up and spoils service

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the letters read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Rev, reverend, is a vicar's title
a haul is a load of loot or spoils

explanation.surface: An aged clergyman stands up and ruins the church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' looks churchy but is a car service; 'spoils' is a noun, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough overhaul of a machine is a full service or repair.

clue.text: Hank Williams's last relatives touring Europe

indicators.note: last picks the final letter of the name Williams
the relatives word tours round the Europe letter, enclosing it

parts.note: kin are relatives

explanation.surface: Country singer Hank Williams's family travel around Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hank' is not the singer Hank Williams but a hank of yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: A hank of yarn and a skein are both coiled lengths of thread.

clue.text: Doctor and nurse go travelling

indicators.note: travelling letters move around into a new order

explanation.surface: A medic and a nurse set off on a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon is a medical practitioner who operates, a kind of doctor.

clue.text: Quietly entering self-help group with your old lack of emotion

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it

parts.note: AA, Alcoholics Anonymous, is a self-help group
P, piano, is the musical direction to play quietly
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Someone slips quietly into a support meeting with an antique sort of indifference.
explanation.definitionFit: Indifference or absence of feeling is the plain dictionary sense of the word.

clue.text: Driver in desert arrived with lascivious look

parts.note: came means arrived
a leer is a lustful sidelong look

explanation.surface: A lorry driver in the Sahara turns up with a suggestive glance.
explanation.definitionFit: A camel driver is the one who drives animals across the desert, a witty take on driver.

clue.text: Brilliant reworking of Mantel book

indicators.note: a reworking rewrites and rearranges the letters

explanation.surface: A dazzling adaptation of a Hilary Mantel novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambent means softly glowing or flickering, and figuratively brilliant or radiant.

clue.text: Not supposed to follow team of stars

indicators.note: the word for not supposed is set to follow the word for team

parts.note: a side is a team
real things are actual, not merely supposed

explanation.surface: Something genuine must come after the team of star players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team of stars' looks like one phrase, but the split falls after 'team'.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers use the adjective for anything measured relative to the fixed stars, as in sidereal time.

clue.text: Women's joint complaint

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors
a hinge is a joint, as of a door or the knee

explanation.surface: Women share a grievance about a sore joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A whinge is British slang for a moan or a peevish grumble.

clue.text: Routes and fare stages

definitions.meaning: paths or tracks taken, as a ship's
fare as food: the stages of a meal, such as starter and main

explanation.surface: Bus routes and their fare stages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare stages' reads as bus fares, but fare is food here.
explanation.definitionFit: Courses are both the routes taken and the successive dishes of a meal.

clue.text: Twelve regularly skipping into town

indicators.note: skipping every other letter at a regular interval keeps the even ones

explanation.surface: A dozen people skip merrily into town.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock midday is a time of day expressed as a number.

clue.text: Release lions, about to be mauled

indicators.note: mauled letters are torn about and rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to free the lions, who are about to maul someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to be mauled' reads as one phrase, but 'about' is fodder alongside 'lions'.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolution is release from guilt or sin, a formal forgiveness.

clue.text: Dull single grandma and I have sex

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one, means single
nan is a British word for grandma
to mate is to have sex

explanation.surface: An absurd confession that a lonely grandmother and the speaker sleep together.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifeless or spiritless, as something dull and without animation is.

clue.text: Intimidate poltroons, lacking guts and oddly touchy

indicators.note: a word lacking its guts keeps only its outer letters
oddly means the letters are arranged in an odd, strange order

explanation.surface: Cowards with no courage behaving in a strangely sensitive way try to scare someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking guts' fits poltroons, cowards, as a description, but it signals removing their middles. 'Oddly' here is an anagram, not alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To psych someone out is to unnerve them psychologically, an idiom for intimidating them.

clue.text: Polite remark from student in class

indicators.note: in puts the student's letter inside the class word

parts.note: the peasantry is a social class
L, from learner plates, stands for a student

explanation.surface: A courteous comment made by a pupil in the classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class' suggests a school lesson but is a social class here.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasantry is a courteous or joking social remark.

clue.text: Prowling Peruvian bear losing weight

indicators.note: the bear's name loses the weight word

parts.note: Paddington Bear came from darkest Peru in the children's stories
a ton is a weight

explanation.surface: A bear from Peru roaming about while shedding pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Padding is walking softly and stealthily, much as a prowling animal moves.

clue.text: Father and married son leaving plains

indicators.note: the married and son letters leave the word for plains

parts.note: the pampas are the grassy plains of South America

explanation.surface: A dad and his newly-wed son depart the prairies.
explanation.walkthrough: The PAMPAS are the South American grasslands; take away M and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is a familiar or childish word for a dad.

clue.text: Very bad baby's malodorous clothes

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here: the words clothe, or wrap round, the answer

explanation.surface: An infant's smelly outfit is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun but is a verb: the words clothe the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal means appallingly poor, dreadful in quality.

clue.text: Mormon half-cut on beer and spirits

indicators.note: half-cut means half of the word is cut, keeping its first half

parts.note: ale is a beer

explanation.surface: A teetotal Mormon gets drunk on beer and spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, but it means cut in half. 'Spirits' is not liquor but mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Morale is a group's confidence or spirits, as in high spirits.

clue.text: Infer two diamonds held

indicators.note: the card-two word holds the diamonds letter inside it

parts.note: a deuce is a two in cards or dice
D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games

explanation.surface: A card player works out that an opponent holds two diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two diamonds' looks like a pair, but 'two' is DEUCE, a card of value two.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce is to reason out a conclusion, the same as to infer it.

clue.text: Stop cleaners ignoring men's toilets

indicators.note: ignoring means the toilet word is left out

parts.note: detergents are cleaning agents
the gents is British slang for a men's lavatory

explanation.surface: Office cleaners told to stop skipping the men's lavatories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaners' suggests people but here means cleaning products.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter is to discourage or prevent, so stop someone acting.

clue.text: Wildness of female erotic dancing ending in orgy

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order
ending in points to the final letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An abandoned scene: a woman's sexy dance finishing in an orgy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferocity is savage fierceness, the untamed quality of a wild animal.

clue.text: Motor racing roots of veteran champion Raikkonen?

definitions.text: Motor racing roots of veteran champion Raikkonen?

parts.words: Motor racing roots of veteran champion Raikkonen?
parts.note: Kimi Raikkonen, the 2007 Formula One champion, comes from Finland, so his national roots name him

explanation.surface: A question about where the Formula One world champion Kimi Raikkonen began his racing career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roots' looks like early career but means his national origins.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Finland, where Raikkonen comes from, is a description of his nationality.

clue.text: Grant entry to hidden parts of wintry home city

indicators.note: the hidden inner parts of each word are what is left once its outer letters are removed

explanation.surface: Someone is let into the secret corners of a cold home town.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word loses its first and last letters: INTR, OM and IT. 'Hidden' looks like a hidden-word signal, but here it means the concealed middles.
explanation.definitionFit: An old, rare verb meaning to admit or let in, from Latin intromittere, to send in.

clue.text: Greeting sadly returned in the morning

indicators.note: returned means the word for sadly is turned back to front

parts.note: alas is an exclamation said sadly
AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning

explanation.surface: A greeting was given back sorrowfully before noon.
explanation.definitionFit: A salaam is a low bow of greeting in Muslim and Indian custom.

clue.text: Extremely giddy sailor pirouetting

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a rating is a naval sailor without a commission

explanation.surface: A very dizzy seaman spinning on the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning round on the spot, as a dancer does in a pirouette, is turning in circles.

clue.text: Drew skinned aquatic mammal in close up again

indicators.note: a skinned word has its outer letters peeled off

parts.note: a seal is an aquatic mammal

explanation.surface: Someone called Drew skinned a seal before stitching it closed again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drew' looks like a verb but is the name, losing D and W.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut or fasten something a second time, as with an opened envelope.
